results.title: Aoun: Diplomacy Does Not Mean Surrender
results.description: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun defended on Tuesday the option of direct negotiations with Israel, stressing that resorting to diplomacy is neither surrender nor defeat, but rather a means of achieving Lebanon’s objectives and restoring its rights. He stated that “diplomacy is not surrender; it is one of the instruments and options of politics. Negotiation is not a sign of weakness, and peace does not compromise dignity.”

results.title: UNRWA Situation Report #239 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem) [EN/AR]
results.description: Please refer to the attached files. Highlights The Gaza Strip As reported by OCHA, recent rains affected more than 220,000 people and damaged over 40,000 shelters, 960 latrines, nine health facilities, and a number of temporary learning spaces across the Gaza Strip. While some UNRWA emergency shelters were temporarily used by some newly displaced families, safe alternative shelter remains extremely limited across Gaza, leaving many affected families with nowhere suitable to relocate. Inter-agency estimates assessed that over 5,000 people were reportedly sleeping in the open after the first rainfall. The scale of needs continues to exceed the response capacity. Humanitarian partners, including UNRWA, are undertaking drainage, debris clearance and identifying alternative shelter for households in flood-prone sites and unsafe buildings. The response remains constrained by severe shortages of heavy machinery, engine oil and spare parts, pumps, and other essential supplies. In partnership with other humanitarian agencies, UNRWA’s teams on the ground are distributing 40,000 winter clothing kits across Gaza, while preparing the distribution of approximately 10,000 tarpaulins and 150 tents to families with the most urgent shelter needs. Israeli forces have continued to reinforce positions along the so-called Yellow Line of Israeli control in the Gaza Strip, with increased tank movements and shooting reported across multiple areas. The resulting insecurity has led to temporary suspensions of UNRWA humanitarian and programme activities, particularly in Khan Younis, Bureij, and Maghazi. Stray-bullet fire remains a growing protection concern, affecting displaced persons, humanitarian facilities, and operations well beyond areas adjacent to the Yellow Line. During October alone, UNRWA recorded one person killed and 14 injured inside its emergency shelters. The pattern continued in November, with a five-year-old child injured at an UNRWA shelter in Khan Younis during the reporting period. On 7 November, a new health centre was established within the Gaza Training Centre to enhance the delivery of essential healthcare services to the population of Gaza City, estimated at more than 670,000 people. Over the reporting period, UNRWA also opened a new temporary learning space at the Rawafid displacement site in northern Rafah, with more than 1,000 children attending in-person education during its first week. Key Points Fatalities and injuries Between 7 October 2023 and 15 November 2026, according to the Ministry of Health (MoH), as reported by the Health Cluster, 74,702 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 176,105 were injured. This includes 1,650 fatalities and 6,144 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 15 November 2026. UNRWA has recorded 395 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 84 persons who were supporting UNRWA[2]), as of 11 November. Health crisis Health facilities across Gaza reported a sharp rise in probable meningitis cases since August, with suspected viral cases 2.6 times and bacterial cases 4.1 times higher than the same period in 2025. In response, UNRWA’s health teams are strengthening surveillance and case detection, verifying vaccination status, reinforcing referral arrangements and infection prevention measures, and coordinating closely with the Ministry of Health and health partners. No outbreak has been declared, also pending further analysis. WASH needs According to the WASH Cluster’s Light Touch Monitoring Survey, completed in October, 85 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene. Water insecurity thus remains a significant concern. Access to basic hygiene supplies also remained severely constrained, with 76 per cent of households reporting insufficient access to essential hygiene items. Displacement, site management UNRWA continues to monitor the movement of displaced persons and displacement sites. A total of 113 UNRWA collective emergency shelters host approximately 60,000 internally displaced persons. Shelter needs According to the Shelter Cluster’s latest Fact Sheet of October 2026, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance.

results.title: Ukraine Shelter Cluster: Winterization Recommendations 2026 - 2027 (Version 1.1)
results.description: Please refer to the attached file. Context It is estimated that since February 2022, around 14 percent of Ukraine’s housing stock has been damaged or destroyed, affecting more than three million households. According to the Fifth Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA5), released in February 2026 and covering the period to 31 December 2025, total direct damage across all sectors has reached approximately USD 195 billion – around 11 percent higher than reported in RDNA4 – with housing remaining the single most affected sector. Housing accounts for roughly 31 percent of total damage, and more than 80 percent of that damage and destruction is concentrated in frontline and border regions. Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, intensified attacks caused further damage to housing and civilian infrastructure across the east, south and north of the country, increasing the number of people displaced from their homes and in need of thermally insulated shelter. The security situation in Donetska, Kharkivska, Zaporizka and Dnipropetrovska oblasts continued to deteriorate, with evacuations ongoing. Since 1 June 2025, according to government figures, around 150,000 people were evacuated from frontline areas to safer regions, including approximately 18,000 children and more than 5,000 persons with limited mobility; further mandatory evacuations with children from frontline settlements in Donetska, Dnipropetrovska, Zaporizka, Kharkivska and Chernihivska oblasts were ordered in the first half of 2026. The winter of 2025–2026 was one of the harshest in recent years and proved detrimental to internally displaced persons (IDPs), non-displaced people in war-affected areas, returnees and host communities alike. More than 3.7 million people remained internally displaced, many having been displaced multiple times. The repair and rehabilitation of collective sites are vital life-saving interventions, as the increasing number of displaced persons and repeated re-damage to previously rehabilitated sites continue to outpace available capacity. Disruptions to centralized and electric heating systems had a profound impact on affected populations during the 2025–2026 season. Between October 2025 and February 2026, coordinated strikes reportedly caused a generation deficit of around 7 GW, and in January 2026 near-daily attacks damaged or destroyed energy assets in at least 17 regions and Kyiv city, leaving millions of people with only a few hours of electricity per day and disrupting heating and water services, particularly in multi-apartment buildings. In early October 2025, the largest attack on Ukraine’s gas infrastructure since the start of the full-scale invasion took an estimated 60 percent of domestic gas production offline. District heating networks remained highly vulnerable – a single damaged facility can interrupt services for entire neighborhoods – and even where infrastructure was operational, heating often remained economically inaccessible due to rising tariffs, irregular income and depleted savings. Based on operational experience from the 2024–2025 and 2025–2026 winter response seasons, solid fuel remained a critical heating solution in both rural and urban areas. Both in-kind distributions and cash assistance proved effective, with the choice of modality largely determined by market functionality and access constraints. In-kind support was often required in remote and frontline locations where fuel markets were disrupted, access was restricted, or insecurity prevented supplier deliveries. Damage to transport infrastructure further disrupted supply chains and increased delivery costs. Where markets are functioning, cash assistance remains the preferred modality, as it provides households with greater flexibility and dignity in meeting their heating needs. To maximize its effectiveness, cash assistance should be accompanied by clear guidance and communication about its intended purpose and appropriate messaging about heating-related expenditures, including recommended fuel quantities and safe, efficient firewood use. Given the consistent wintertime targeting of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and the recurring inoperability of heating systems during the coldest months, solid fuel and stoves (including fittings and installation equipment) must continue to be prioritized, irrespective of ongoing price fluctuations. Damage and lack of maintenance have affected heating systems in collective sites and in individual houses and apartments alike; in many cases, these systems – including water heaters, electrical grids, gas and hot-water pipelines, internal pipes, radiators and stoves – must be reactivated, repaired or replaced. Portable heating appliances should be provided where the heating system is dysfunctional or cannot be restored before the upcoming winter season. One of the most important lessons from the 2025–2026 season is that timing is a core quality standard. Post-distribution monitoring consistently showed that assistance received before the heating season is markedly more effective, whereas delays in implementation and delivery, whether cash transfers or in-kind assistance, forced households to borrow fuel, reduce heating, deplete savings, or purchase at peak prices, and late funding left insufficient lead time for in-kind procurement and delivery. The 2026–2027 response should therefore aim to complete most of the registration, procurement, payments, and in-kind deliveries by October. Lessons learned also reaffirmed the importance of pre-positioning heating appliances and solid fuel in advance of peak winter months, and of giving special attention to female-headed households and elderly individuals, many of whom are unable to physically unload, store or process large firewood deliveries. In addition to heating, essential household items such as warm winter clothing, thermal underwear and thermal blankets remain necessary for displaced individuals, returnees and others who have lost their belongings, lack access to markets, or cannot afford essential winter items. Interventions should be based on a sex- and age-disaggregated household needs assessment, in line with agreed vulnerability criteria, and may be delivered in-kind or through cash/voucher assistance, wherever feasible and appropriate, particularly for winter preparations. Assistance continued to be guided by the principle of deduplication. The combined use of winter coordination tables and the RAIS+ platform – used by more than 78 partners – enabled coordinated assistance to over 357,000 households and prevented an estimated USD 45 million in duplicate payments during the 2025–2026 season. Accurate and timely reporting by partners into RAIS+ remains crucial for cross-checking and ensuring harmonized coverage, both within and between clusters. This guidance is framed within the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP), which estimates that 10.8 million people require humanitarian assistance in 2026 and prioritizes 4.1 million of the most vulnerable. In light of the evolving context and operational lessons from 2025– 2026, the Shelter and NFI Cluster has further adjusted its planning assumptions and priorities for the 2026–2027 winterization response, emphasizing early preparedness, earlier procurement and pre-positioning, stronger and earlier coordination with governmental actors at oblast and hromada levels, improved targeting and deduplication mechanisms, diversified delivery modalities tailored to market constraints, and the explicit integration of energy-shock preparedness. Contextual risks – energy infrastructure disruptions, fluctuating fuel markets and recurring displacement – should be explicitly factored into planning, including pre-positioning in high-risk areas, contingency planning for shifts between cash and in-kind modalities, and flexibility to adapt to changing market and security conditions.

results.title: 79th Anniversary of Mirpur Massacre of 1947: Annihilated, still alive
results.description: Every year on November 25, displaced families from Mirpur & Pakistan-Occupied Jammu & Kashmir (POJK) observe Mirpur Fall Day. To the outside world, it passes as an obscure calendar entry. To hundreds of thousands of survivors and their descendants, it marks an unhealed wound—seventy-nine years of violent dispossession, diplomatic amnesia, and institutional neglect. On November 25, 1947, following weeks of relentless siege during the Pakistani tribal invasion, the historic town of Mirpur fell. What followed was not mere collateral damage of war, but a systematic campaign of mass slaughter, mass abduction, plunder, and forced expulsion. Hindu and Sikh minorities were hunted down because of their faith. Women were abducted and subjected to unspeakable atrocities; community elders, professionals, and civic leaders were executed. Overnight, ancient communities across Mirpur, Bhimber, Kotli, Muzaffarabad, and Poonch were stripped of their homes, businesses, fertile lands, and sacred shrines—driven out with nothing left but the clothes on their backs. These were not voluntary migrations. This was the violent uprooting of an indigenous population, left to rebuild from ashes while the world looked away. Nehru’s Telegram: Smoking Gun in Official Archives The atrocity of Mirpur is neither folklore nor partisan exaggeration. It is etched in black and white in highest diplomatic records of independent India. On December 2, 1947,—barely seven days after Mirpur fell—India’s first PM, Jawaharlal Nehru, sent an urgent cable directly to Pakistani PM Liaquat Ali Khan. Preserved in the Nehru Archive and reproduced in Government of India’s White Paper on Jammu and Kashmir, Nehru’s dispatch stated unequivocally that “Mirpur town has been completely destroyed.” He recorded that out of 13,000 non-Muslims, a mere 2,000 had survived to reach within fifteen miles of Jhelum, while sounding the alarm over thousands of missing refugees and reports of large numbers of abducted Hindu women being marched into the Jhelum district. This was contemporaneous diplomatic evidence sent as the blood was still drying. It leaves policymakers and historians with a damning question: When the Prime Minister of India formally placed this mass atrocity on record in December 1947, what excuses seventy-nine years of inaction and silence? Read More: Thiruparankundram Drepathoon Row: VHP accuses TVK of continuing anti-Sanatan politics of DMK, seeks SC action Silence of International Community For nearly eight decades, the United Nations and global human rights institutions have dissected the territorial dispute over Jammu and Kashmir from every geopolitical angle—yet they have maintained a deafening silence on the ethnic cleansing of Mirpur’s Hindu and Sikh minorities. Survivors and their descendants have long asserted that their communities were targeted for total eradication based on religious identity. The scale of the killings, the organised abduction of women, and the permanent expulsion of entire populations bear every hallmark of genocidal persecution—crimes that demand independent international investigation and scrutiny under the UN Genocide Convention. Selective human rights advocacy is a betrayal of human dignity. A people robbed of their homeland cannot be erased a second time from global conscience. Seventy-Nine Years of Bureaucratic Cruelty Today, almost the entire generation that survived the horrors of 1947 has passed away without ever seeing justice. Their children and grandchildren have inherited not only the trauma of exile, but the burden of fighting a rigid, indifferent bureaucracy. Official figures tabled before the Indian Parliament acknowledge 31,619 registered displaced families from POJK—26,319 in Jammu and Kashmir and 5,300 scattered across other states. Yet these figures expose a glaring administrative failure: ● Uncounted Thousands: Countless families fled directly to Delhi, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, and beyond in sheer terror, bypassing formal camp registries. ● Fractured Families: Joint households were torn apart during the exodus, leaving entire branches permanently locked out of official rolls. When families fled burning towns to save their lives, carrying property deeds and registration slips was impossible. To deny a victim’s descendant their birth right today because their grandparents lacked paperwork in 1947 is bureaucratic cruelty. The absence of a paper slip does not erase a historical truth. Drowned Beneath the Mangla Dam For the people of Mirpur, exile was followed by literal annihilation of their homeland. Between 1961 and 1967, Pakistan constructed the Mangla Dam on the Jhelum River inside occupied territory. Its massive reservoir submerged the historic city of Mirpur, dozens of surrounding villages, and vast tracts of ancestral farmland. For families already driven out in 1947, this was an irreversible final blow. Their ancestral homes, neighbourhoods, mandirs, and heritage vanished beneath deep water—extinguishing even the physical possibility of return. First they were expelled from their land; then their land itself was drowned. Betrayal of Third Generation The Union Government’s 2016 approval of a one-time financial grant of Rs 5.5 lakh per eligible family was a belated acknowledgment—but token compensation cannot pass for comprehensive rehabilitation. Unresolved land rights, missing records, split family claims, and the exclusion of families outside Jammu and Kashmir continue to leave thousands in limbo. Meanwhile, a third generation has come of age. Born in independent India solely because their grandparents were violently expelled from POJK, these young citizens are entering universities, professions, and public life with zero structural recognition of their historical displacement. They do not ask for charity or sporadic handouts; they demand permanent, enforceable rights. Five Non-Negotiable Demands Sympathy without policy is empty rhetoric. The Government of India must immediately constitute an empowered, time-bound committee—with representation from displaced families and domain experts—to execute five concrete measures: Restore Meaningful Political Representation: Act on the 2014 Parliamentary Standing Committee recommendation to defreeze eight Assembly seats for POJK displaced persons. One nominated representative under the 2023 amendment is symbolic; a community of over a million displaced citizens demands substantive legislative power. Guarantee National Educational Access: Establish a dedicated educational framework for eligible children and grandchildren of POJK displaced families—including supernumerary seats, scholarships, and fee concessions across central universities, IITs, NITs, medical colleges, and premier institutions nationwide, irrespective of their state of residence. Create Targeted Employment Pathways: Introduce special employment-support measures, including age and fee relaxations, for eligible descendants in central government services and public sector undertakings […]

results.title: Venezuela reveals US$237.5bil debt pile in key step towards restructuring
results.description: CARACAS/LONDON/NEW YORK: Venezuela’s government put its total debt at US$237.5 billion in a long-awaited macroeconomic framework published on Tuesday, providing the clearest picture in years of the country’s shattered finances and a potential foundation for one of the world’s largest-ever debt restructurings.
